hero.name: Raju
hero.who: a software tester in Hyderabad with a good salary and almost no savings

story.b: Raju earns more than his father ever did. He tests software for a company in Hitech City, shares a flat in Kondapur with two friends, and rides a new bike on EMI. Every weekend there is a cafe, a movie or a trip to some resort. His phone is the latest model. By the twenty-fifth of each month his account is almost empty, and he waits for the first like a schoolboy waiting for pocket money. He thinks of himself as doing well. Then his flatmate's car breaks down and needs forty thousand rupees in repairs. Raju realises he could not pay that amount for himself, let alone lend it.

ask.q: Raju feels successful but could not handle a forty thousand rupee emergency. What does this most likely show?
o: He needs a higher-paying job before he can save anything
Looking well-off and actually being financially secure are different things
Emergencies are rare, so there is nothing to worry about
ask.why: His lifestyle looks prosperous, but security comes from what he has kept, not what he shows. A bigger salary often just grows the spending with it. And emergencies are not rare at all. The gap between looking fine and being fine is exactly what he needs to notice.

chapters.take: Looking rich and being rich are not the same thing.

story.h: The colleague with the steel dabba
story.b: At the office, Raju has always felt a little sorry for Srinivas, a senior tester who takes the metro, carries lunch in a steel dabba and wears the same three shirts. One Friday, Srinivas mentions that he has just finished paying for his flat in Miyapur, years ahead of schedule. Raju is stunned. That same week, another colleague, Vikram, who drives a big car and posts holiday photos every month, quietly asks Raju for a small loan to cover his credit card bill. Raju walks home thinking about both men. He had judged their money entirely by what he could see. What he could see had told him almost nothing.

ask.q: Raju's cousin assumes a classmate's family is rich because of their big car and parties. What would Raju now say?
o: Appearances can hide debts, so you cannot judge wealth by what you see
A big car is clear proof of a big bank balance
Rich people always show off, so quiet people must be poor
ask.why: Spending can be seen, but saving is invisible. A big car might be fully paid for or sitting on a large EMI. Many quietly comfortable people choose to live plainly. Judging wealth by display leads you to copy the wrong people and to feel poorer than you are.

chapters.take: Wealth is usually quiet. What you see is spending, not savings.

story.h: Nine lakhs in, very little kept
story.b: One Sunday Raju downloads a year of bank statements and adds it all up on a sheet of paper. He earned a little over nine lakh rupees after tax last year. He kept twenty-six thousand. He reads the number twice. Where did it all go? Rent, the bike EMI, food delivery almost every night, weekend trips, a new phone, gifts, subscriptions he had forgotten about. None of it felt wasteful at the time. He thinks of Srinivas, who probably earned less than him for years and now owns a flat. Raju realises his salary had made him feel rich, while the habit of keeping money was what actually built wealth.

ask.q: Raju gets a twenty percent raise next month. What is the smartest thing to do with it?
o: Upgrade his bike, since he has earned a reward
Spend more freely, since his income is now higher
Set aside most of the raise automatically, before he gets used to it
ask.why: Income becomes wealth only if some of it is kept. Moving most of the raise into savings before his lifestyle adjusts means he builds wealth without feeling poorer. Upgrading the bike or spending freely turns a bigger income into bigger bills, and he ends up where he started.

chapters.take: What you keep matters more than what you earn.

story.b: Raju writes down every rupee he spends for one month in a small notebook. The surprise is food delivery: nearly eleven thousand rupees, mostly late at night when he was too tired to cook. He and his flatmates start cooking dal and rice together on weeknights, taking turns. He cancels three subscriptions he never watches. He keeps the things he truly enjoys, like his Saturday badminton game and one good meal out each week. He sets up an automatic SIP into an index fund on the second of every month, the day after his salary arrives. By the end of the month he feels lighter, not poorer, as if money has stopped slipping through his fingers.

ask.q: Raju's flatmate wants to save by cutting every single pleasure, even chai with friends. What would Raju suggest?
o: Cut everything, because any spending is a waste
Make a budget, trim what he does not value, and keep a few real joys
Give up on saving, since living cheaply is miserable
ask.why: Living below your means is about choosing, not suffering. A budget shows where money leaks, so he can cut what he does not care about and keep what he does. Cutting every joy often ends in a spending binge, and giving up means losing the freedom that saving brings.

chapters.take: Frugal living means spending on what matters to you, and little else.

story.b: Three people in Raju's team buy new cars within two months. Every lunch conversation turns to sunroofs and touchscreens. His mother calls to say his cousin in Warangal has bought one too. Raju starts feeling his bike looks shabby in the office parking. One evening he finds himself on a car website, choosing colours for a loan he cannot really afford. He stops and asks who he is buying it for. Not for his commute. The bike works perfectly. He is buying it for the parking lot, for lunch conversations and for his cousin. He closes the website. He also mutes a few car-review channels he watches late at night.

ask.q: Raju's friends are planning a costly weekend trip he cannot afford, and he fears being left out. What should he do?
o: Be honest, skip this one, and suggest a cheaper plan they can all enjoy
Go anyway and put the whole trip on his credit card
Make up an excuse, so nobody knows money is the reason
ask.why: Keeping up with other people's spending is one of the quickest ways to stay broke. Being honest and offering a cheaper plan protects both his goals and his friendships. Charging it creates debt for one weekend, and excuses keep him trapped in the same pressure next time.

chapters.take: Stop keeping up with others. Keep up with your own goals instead.

story.b: When Raju visits home in Guntur for Sankranti, his father notices the old bike and offers to pay for a car. Appa saved carefully all his life as a government clerk, and he says it would make him happy to help his son. Raju is touched. A year ago he would have said yes at once. But he also remembers how, in college, Appa's monthly top-ups meant he never learned to manage money himself. If his father pays for this, he will need help for the next big thing too. Raju thanks him and says no. Instead, he asks Appa to sit with him and explain how he managed to save on a clerk's salary.

ask.q: Raju's aunt keeps paying her grown-up son's credit card bills, and he keeps spending. What would truly help him most?
o: Pay the bills quietly so he does not feel stressed
Increase the support so he never falls short
Gradually stop paying, and help him learn to manage his own money
ask.why: Regular handouts to a grown child can weaken his drive and skill to handle money. Stepping back gradually, while helping him learn budgeting, builds independence. Paying quietly or increasing support may feel loving, but it keeps him dependent and makes the spending habit stronger.

chapters.take: Teaching money independence is a bigger gift than paying the bills.

story.b: Eight months later, the twenty-fifth of the month feels different for Raju. There is still money in his account. His SIP has gone in quietly every month, and he has an emergency fund big enough for three months of expenses. He still rides the same bike and still plays badminton every Saturday. Two of his teammates who bought new cars now complain about EMIs at lunch. Srinivas has become a friend and lends him books on personal finance. When his younger sister starts her first job in Bengaluru, Raju does not send her money. He sends her a photo of his spending notebook, and a message suggesting she keep one too.

chapters.take: Wealth is built quietly, by keeping more than you show.
